title: Nutrition and Dietetics Basics
summary: Learn the science of nutrition: nutrients and energy, carbohydrates, proteins and fats, micronutrients and deficiencies, balanced diets through life, nutrition assessment and diet-related disease, and food safety and security.
audience: Health and nutrition students, community health workers, cooks, parents and anyone interested in healthy eating

body.p: Nutrition is how the body uses food for energy, growth, repair and protection against disease. Dietetics applies nutrition science to feed individuals and groups well, in health and illness. Registered dietitians are trained and licensed to give individual dietary treatment; this course gives general education.

list: Carbohydrates: the main energy source (maize, rice, cassava, bread, fruit). Whole grains also give fibre.
Proteins: for growth and repair (beans, lentils, groundnuts, eggs, fish, meat, milk).
Fats: concentrated energy and fat-soluble vitamins (oils, nuts, seeds, fish).
Vitamins and minerals (micronutrients): needed in small amounts for many body functions.
Water and fibre: essential for hydration and healthy digestion.

body.p: Energy is measured in kilocalories (kcal) or kilojoules (1 kcal is about 4.2 kJ). Carbohydrate and protein give about 4 kcal per gram, fat about 9 kcal per gram and alcohol about 7. A meal with 60 g of carbohydrate, 20 g of protein and 15 g of fat provides 60 x 4 + 20 x 4 + 15 x 9 = 455 kcal, with fat supplying 135 kcal, about 29.7% of the energy.

body.tip: Energy needs vary widely with age, body size, activity, pregnancy and illness; there is no single right number for everyone.

lessons.title: Carbohydrates, proteins and fats in detail

body.p: Not all sources of each macronutrient are equal for health.

list: Carbohydrates: choose mostly whole grains, legumes, vegetables and fruit; limit added sugars and sugary drinks, which give energy without other nutrients and harm teeth.
Fibre helps digestion, keeps blood sugar steadier and supports heart health; it comes from whole grains, beans, vegetables and fruit.

Proteins: animal foods provide all essential amino acids; plant proteins can do so too when combined, such as maize with beans or rice with lentils. A common reference for adults is about 0.8 g of protein per kg of body weight a day, about 48 g for a 60 kg adult, more in pregnancy, growth and some illnesses.
Fats: unsaturated fats (vegetable oils, nuts, fish) are healthier than saturated fats (fatty meat, butter, palm and coconut oil in large amounts); industrial trans fats should be avoided.

body.p: Traditional diets based on grains, legumes, vegetables and some animal foods are often healthy; rising intake of processed foods high in sugar, salt and unhealthy fats is driving diet-related disease in many countries.

body.tip: Read ingredient lists: ingredients are listed from most to least by weight, so sugar near the top means a lot of sugar.

body.p: Micronutrient deficiencies, sometimes called hidden hunger, affect many people, especially children and women of reproductive age.

list: Iron: needed for red blood cells; deficiency causes anaemia, tiredness and poorer learning. Sources: meat, fish, legumes, dark green leaves; vitamin C improves absorption from plants.
Vitamin A: vision and immunity; deficiency causes night blindness and more severe infections. Sources: orange vegetables and fruit, dark leafy greens, liver, eggs, red palm oil.
Iodine: thyroid function and brain development; iodised salt is the main prevention.
Zinc: growth and immunity; important in treating childhood diarrhoea.
Folate: prevents some birth defects; recommended before and during early pregnancy.
Calcium and vitamin D: bones and teeth; sunlight helps the body make vitamin D.

body.p: Countries fight deficiencies through food fortification (adding iodine to salt, vitamin A to oil, iron and folic acid to flour), supplementation programmes for children and pregnant women, and promoting diverse diets, including bio-fortified crops such as orange-fleshed sweet potato.

body.tip: A colourful plate with several food groups each day is the simplest way to cover most micronutrients.

lessons.title: Balanced diets across the life course

body.p: A balanced diet includes a variety of foods from several groups: starchy staples (preferably whole grain), vegetables and fruit, legumes and nuts, animal-source foods where available, and small amounts of healthy oils, with plenty of clean water.

list: Infants: exclusive breastfeeding for about the first 6 months, then nutritious complementary foods while breastfeeding continues, as WHO recommends.
Children and adolescents: energy and protein for growth, iron, calcium and regular meals, including breakfast.
Pregnancy and breastfeeding: extra energy, protein, iron, folate, iodine and calcium.
Older adults: smaller appetites but similar or greater needs for protein, calcium, vitamin D and B12; watch for poor intake.

body.p: WHO recommends adults eat less than 5 g of salt a day. Food labels often show sodium: salt is about 2.5 times the sodium, so 2 g of sodium equals about 5 g of salt. A product with 2.4 g of sodium contains about 6 g of salt, more than a full day's limit.

body.tip: Plan meals around affordable local foods: beans, groundnuts, eggs, small fish, leafy greens and seasonal fruit are nutritious and often cheaper than processed alternatives.

body.p: Health workers assess nutrition through history (what and how much a person eats), measurements, clinical signs and sometimes blood tests.

list: Body mass index (BMI) = weight (kg) / height (m)². A 70 kg adult who is 1.75 m tall has a BMI of 70 / 1.75², about 22.9. BMI is a screening tool for adults and does not measure body fat directly.
Children are assessed with growth charts (weight-for-age, height-for-age, weight-for-height) because they are growing.
Mid-upper-arm circumference (MUAC) tapes quickly screen children for acute malnutrition in communities.
Waist circumference indicates abdominal fat linked to heart disease and diabetes.

body.p: Type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease and some cancers are linked to diets high in sugar, salt, processed and fatty foods and low in vegetables, fruit, legumes and whole grains, together with physical inactivity, smoking and alcohol. Many countries now face undernutrition and overweight at the same time, sometimes within one household.

body.tip: Anyone with a medical condition, pregnancy, an eating difficulty or concerns about their weight or eating should get individual advice from a doctor or registered dietitian.

lessons.title: Food safety, food security and careers

body.p: Safe food is as important as nutritious food. Unsafe food causes diarrhoeal disease and other illnesses, especially in children.

body.h: WHO's five keys to safer food

list: Keep clean: wash hands and surfaces.
Separate raw and cooked food.
Cook thoroughly, especially meat, eggs and seafood.
Keep food at safe temperatures; do not leave cooked food at room temperature for more than about 2 hours.
Use safe water and raw materials.

body.p: Food security means everyone always has access to enough safe, nutritious food. It depends on production, incomes, prices, markets, storage, climate and conflict. Nutrition-sensitive agriculture, social protection and school feeding programmes all help.

Nutrition professionals work as registered dietitians in hospitals and clinics, public-health nutritionists, food-service managers, food scientists, community nutrition workers and researchers. Titles such as "dietitian" are often protected by law and need accredited degrees and registration.

body.tip: Be cautious of nutrition advice on social media that promises quick cures or sells supplements; look for qualified sources.
